video_title: How to Survive a Collapsing Sand Dune
text: Sand dunes. These breathtaking, gigantic structures formed by tiny grains of sand are beautiful until you're being swallowed by one. Deserts are dangerous. If you don’t watch your step, you could end up buried alive.

video_title: How to Survive a Collapsing Sand Dune
text: A dune is a mound of sand formed when the wind blows grains of sand into a sheltered area. Dunes have a slip face, the side that's sheltered from the wind, and a windward side where the wind pushes material. When the slope becomes greater than 34 degrees, gravity pulls the loose sand down, causing slumping. "We have to get out of here" Sand dunes are marketed as tourist destinations. But sand is an unstable substance that can collapse quickly without any warning, swallowing people in seconds. Nothing says your vacation is over like being trapped in a dune that's 0.5 km (0.3 mi) high, huh?

video_title: How to Survive a Collapsing Sand Dune
text: The biggest dunes can have nearly 5 billion m² (169.5 billion ft²) of sand. If you find yourself trapped inside a dune, try to stay quiet and calm. Every orifice of your body will be bombarded by grains of sand. “Sand in my eyes!” And breathing heavily or screaming will help sand enter your lungs faster, which is painful and dangerous.

video_title: How to Survive a Collapsing Sand Dune
text: Mount Baldy, in Indiana, is 38 m (125 ft) high. In 2013, this huge sand dune swallowed a six-year-old. The boy fell 3.3 m (11 ft) into the sand and remained buried for more than three hours. He only survived because an air pocket formed around him as the sand was collapsing. Even if you’re as lucky as Nathan and have air to breathe, you’ll need to preserve it. Don’t do anything that would use up your oxygen supply quickly, like making intense movements.

video_title: How to Survive a Collapsing Sand Dune
text: Sand dunes are found in deserts and on beaches, and they’re different. “Sand in the eye!” Dunes near the ocean are stationary since the water cements them in place. But in a desert, the dunes travel with the wind, which presents another threat. Wind-blown sand can cause blindness and disorientation. And a dune’s nature is hazardous enough with your two eyes working. If you want to preserve them, you’ll need to keep your eyes closed.

video_title: How to Survive a Collapsing Sand Dune
text: This might sound counterintuitive. But if the sand is fresh, it will fill back in wherever you push it away. If you try digging yourself out, you could end up buried even further down inside the dune.

video_title: How to Survive a Collapsing Sand Dune
text: Some animals can live inside dunes. The sandfish, a type of lizard, can retract its legs and move through the sand. A few species thrive in this environment, but you’re not one of them. If a dune swallows you, it would be tough to find you quickly if people don’t know your location. “Get me out of here!” Always tell people exactly where you're going, so they can send help if you don't return. So, you found a way to survive a collapsing sand dune. But, what about other types of sand? “Quicksand!” Could you survive quicksand? Find out here on How to Survive.
